tagline: Mining towns and forested country lead toward the divide at Yuba Pass
intro: Highway 49 crosses Sierra County through forested terrain, linking Goodyears Bar, Downieville and Sierra City before reaching Yuba Pass. Sierra City sits in the North Yuba River canyon, with the sheer peaks of the Sierra Buttes above town. The stretch from the Sierra–Yuba county line to Yuba Summit is officially designated a scenic highway by the California Department of Transportation. It also belongs to the longer Yuba-Donner National Forest Scenic Byway. Downieville lies at 2,966 feet; Sierra City stands at 4,147 feet, before the route reaches the higher pass.

The mining camps came first; the campaign to connect gold-rush sites by highway began in 1919. The Mother Lode Highway Association, a group of local residents and historians, pressed for the road. The Golden Chain Council promoted the route with a map and tourist guide in 1951, and the entire highway officially became SR 49 in 1963.

From the Yuba County line, drive through Goodyears Bar to Downieville, where the Downie River meets the North Yuba. Continue through Sierra City, where Highway 49 serves as Main Street, then pass Bassetts beside the river. Yuba Pass finishes the climb at 6,710 feet, on the divide between the North Yuba and the Middle Fork Feather River.

moments.title: Goodyears Bar
moments.text: Goodyears Bar stands beside the North Yuba, but prospectors also worked Goodyears Creek. Miles and Andrew Goodyear found gold here in 1849 with Dr. Vaughan and Mr. Morrison. The brothers built a cabin, and the camp took the Goodyear name in honor of its founders. Before 1851 it was known as Slaughter’s Bar. A post office followed in 1851, and the first school began in 1856 with Mrs. Massey as teacher. The community remains on Highway 49 west-southwest of Downieville.

moments.title: Downieville
moments.text: The meeting of the Downie River and North Yuba gave Downieville its first name, The Forks. Founded during the gold rush in late 1849, the settlement had fifteen hotels by 1850. It competed to become California’s state capital in 1853, but the capital moved to Benicia and then Sacramento. Downieville continued as Sierra County’s seat. Its museum occupies an 1852 stone building that began as a general store, with original iron doors and window shutters. Inside is a scale model of the business district at the turn of the twentieth century.

moments.title: Sierra City
moments.text: An ore car and antique mining tools are embedded in the stonework of Sierra City’s post office, dedicated in 1969. They mark a town where hard-rock mines developed on both sides of the North Yuba canyon. The Monumental Nugget, recovered in September 1869, weighed more than 106 pounds. None of the nearby hard-rock mines operates now; the Kentucky mine outside town houses a mining museum. Along Highway 49, the town’s main street, the two-story brick Busch Building survives from the era when Wells Fargo occupied it. Above these streets, the Sierra Buttes rise in a cluster of sheer rock peaks; placer mining continues along the North Yuba’s banks.
moments.notice: Look for the ore car and mining tools embedded in the post office’s stonework.
